title: Engineering 2D Multifunctional Ultrathin Bismuthene for Multiple Photonic Nanomedicine

lanes.label: Classical tools
lanes.sub: collapsed to one node per state

states.title: Hypothesis and design
states.head: Cancer nanomedicine needs one agent that heats, generates ROS and gives imaging contrast under NIR light. Water-mediated freeze-thaw exfoliation plus NaBH4 reduction should give few-layered bismuthene with NIR absorbance for photonic therapy.
states.detail: Absorbed: n1 (HYP/need), n3 (HYP/hypothesis), n4 (DES/base_system), n5 (DES/route), n6 (DES/modification), n7 (DES/variable_sweep), n8 (PRC/treatment), n9 (PRC/synthesis), n10 (PRC/synthesis), n26 (PRC/stimulus)

states.title: Structure state
states.head: Free-standing ultrathin 2D bismuthene nanosheets, ~200 nm lateral size. Reduced sheets are crystalline rhombohedral Bi (PDF#05-0519); the exfoliated precursor is a Bi-oxide phase (PDF#45-1344)

states.title: Property state and mechanisms
states.head: Direct band gap 0.69 eV with broad vis-NIR absorbance; extinction coefficient 6.4 L/g/cm at 808 nm. Narrow-gap ultrathin semiconductor: 808 nm photons relax non-radiatively to heat, 660 nm photons separate e-h pairs that make singlet oxygen.

states.title: Performance state
states.head: BNs-BSA gives concentration-linear photoacoustic contrast and raises tumour CT contrast in vivo. Combined 660 + 808 nm irradiation of BNs-BSA eradicates 4T1 tumours with 100% morbidity-free survival

states.title: Conclusion
states.head: A solvent-free freeze-thaw plus reduction route delivers 2D bismuthene that images and treats tumours by PTT and PDT together

use: TEM images reveal that homogeneous few- or single-layered 2D ultrathin bismuthene oxide nanosheets are stripped off from Bi bulk crystal triumphantly after five cycles of repeated freezing and thawing accompanied with ultrasonic processing (Figure 2a), which feature the typical free-standing nanosheet morphology with relatively high transparency and lateral size of ${\approx}200\mathrm{nm}$ .

It is noted that, after $\mathrm{NaBH_{4}}$ treatment, bismuthene shows distinct lamellar morphology in SEM image (Figure 2b) and $5{-}25~\mathrm{nm}$ ultra-small nanoflakes have grown onto the surface of 2D bismuthene oxide, which distribute uniformly to form heterojunction (Figure 2c).

The atomic-resolution STEM in high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) mode reveals that the as-grown Bi layer is featured with different crystalline structures and the lattice spacing is measure to be 0.227 nm with [110] preferential orientation (Figure 2g,h).

The atomic-resolution STEM in high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) mode reveals that the as-grown Bi layer is featured with different crystalline structures and the lattice spacing is measure to be 0.227 nm with [110] preferential orientation (Figure 2g,h).

According to the XRD patterns (Figure 2k), all diffraction peaks of bismuthene oxide are consistent with the standard $\mathrm{Bi}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{3}$ (JCPDS No. 45-1344) and the typical diffraction peaks of bismuthene are well indexed to the standard hexagonal PDF card (JCPDS No. 05-0519) of Bi.
The average topographic height of bismuthene was acquired to be ${\approx}14$ nm by AFM (Figure 2j), which exhibits prominent lamellar structure.

use: According to the Lambert–Beer law, the extinction coefficient $(\alpha)$ of bismuthene at $808~\mathrm{nm}$ is calculated to be $6.4\mathrm{L}\mathrm{g}^{-1}\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ (Figure 3c),[45] much higher than that of certain representative photothermal agents such as graphene oxide $(3.6\mathrm{~L~g~}^{-1}\mathrm{cm}^{-1})$ ,[46] indicating that 2D bismuthene could serve as a desirable photothermal agent for light-to-heat conversion.

10.1002/adfm.202005093#F3a.definition: Time-dependent absorption spectra of DPBF with bismuthene upon $660~\mathsf{n m}$ laser irradiation and
use: It is obvious that the absorbance at $410\mathrm{nm}$ of the DPBF was gradually weakened with the prolongation of irradiation time of $660~\mathrm{nm}$ laser at $100\mathrm{mW~cm}^{-2}$ , while a slight decline was observed in pure deionized (DI) water with the same laser irradiation, demonstrating the remarkable photodynamic performance of ultrathin bismuthene (Figure 3a,b; Figure S11, Supporting Information).

The temperature of bismuthene aqueous dispersions $(200~\upmu\mathrm{g}~\mathrm{mL}^{-1})$ elevated from 31.7 to $57.7~^{\circ}C$ when irradiated via $808~\mathrm{nm}$ laser $(1.5\mathrm{W}\mathrm{cm}^{-2})$ for 6 min (Figure 3d).

With increased bismuthene concentrations, the temperature of bismuthene aqueous dispersion can increase by $7.4~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for $25~\upmu\mathrm{g}~\mathrm{mL}^{-1}$ , $11.3~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for $50~\upmu\mathrm{g}~\mathrm{mL}^{-1}$ , $16.3~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for $100\upmu\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mL}^{-1}$ , and $27.3~^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for $200\upmu\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mL}^{-1}$ in 6 min (Figure 3d,e).

10.1002/adfm.202005093#F3f.definition: Laser power density dependent temperature-changing curves and
use: In addition, the enhanced photothermal performance can also be achieved by reinforcing radiation power density (Figure 3f,g), further demonstrating the regulable performance of bismuthene in photothermal conversion.

10.1002/adfm.202005093#F3h.definition: Photothermal-heating curve, corresponding cooling process, and relevant linear relationship between $-\ln\theta$ and time
use: The photothermal conversion efficiency $(\eta)$ of the bismuthene was calculated to be $19.4\%$ (Figure 3h),[45] higher than copper nanowires $(12.5\%)$ ,[47] Au nanoshells $(13\%),^{[48]}$ and close to that of traditional graphene-oxide $(22\%)$ .[49] Additionally, neglectable deterioration of the temperature elevation was observed during the cycles of laser on/off irradiation (Figure 3i), highlighting the photo­ stability and thermostability of 2D bismuthene.
The PA signal intensities of BNs-BSA are linearly increased with the elevated nanosheets concentrations (Figure 5c,e).

10.1002/adfm.202005093#F4h.definition: coronal plane images (inset) and corresponding signal intensities of CT imaging before and after intravenous injection
use: The accumulation of BNs-BSA in tumor section provides contrastenhanced CT signals under the irradiation of X-rays, and CT intensities in the tumor region increase over time (Figure 5g,h).

10.1002/adfm.202005093#F5c.definition: the corresponding temperature changes of 4T1-tumor-bearing mice injected with PBS or BNs-BSA under the $808\mathsf{n m}$ laser $(7~\mathsf{W}\thinspace\mathsf{c m}^{-2})$ irradiation for 6 min
use: Meanwhile, thermal images and tumor-site temperature were recorded using an infrared thermal camera (Figure 6b,c).

10.1002/adfm.202005093#F5f.definition: tumor volumes for each group of mice recorded every 2 days after various treatments $(n=5)$
use: After various treatments, the tumor volume (Figure 6d,f) and body weight (Figure 6e) of each mouse were recorded every other day and the photos of tumor sections were recorded every 7 days (Figure S23, Supporting Information).

10.1002/adfm.202005093#F5g.definition: Survival rates of 4T1 tumor-bearing mice in each group with various treatments
use: The PDT treatment resulted in tumor regression of $33.4\%$ compared with the untreated group and the mice in this group died gradually (Figure 6g).
